note: Rewritten from the species-level description of Chhotani (1997), originally in English; alate, soldier and worker all described; synonymy, literature citations, figure numbers and distribution records not translated; one antennal segment count is incomplete in the OCR and that value is not recorded.

sections.label: Soldier
sections.text: Head capsule pale yellowish brown to deep chestnut brown, antennae yellowish brown and darker apically, mandibles reddish brown and paler at base. Cephalic setae sparse, body setae denser. Body length 3.60–5.60 mm. Head capsule broadly oval, widest posteriorly and narrowed anteriorly (head length to mandibular base 1.10–1.35, maximum width 0.95–1.15, width at mandibular base 0.63–0.70 mm; maximum width/length index 0.81–0.93, mandibular base width/maximum width index 0.61–0.70). Antennae 16–17-segmented; with 16 segments segment 4 shortest, with 17 segments segment 3 shortest. Labrum ligulate, anteriorly tapering to a slightly pointed apex. Mandibles short and stout, falcate, strongly incurved apically (length 0.60–0.73 mm), relatively short with respect to head length (mandible length/head length index 0.548–0.583). Left mandible with a large pointed tooth at the apical third (tooth-to-apex distance 0.18–0.25 mm, tooth-to-apex/mandible length index 0.27–0.33); right mandible with a small tooth slightly above midlength. Postmentum subrectangular, sides slightly convex, slightly longer than wide (length 0.60–0.75, maximum width 0.45–0.55 mm). Pronotum saddle-shaped (length 0.40–0.55, width 0.70–0.90 mm), anterior margin weakly concave, posterior margin nearly straight; mesonotum narrower, metanotum wider, posterior margins of both without a concavity.

sections.label: Worker
sections.text: Workers dimorphic. Major worker: head capsule pale yellow to yellowish brown, antennae pale brown and paler at base, body yellow-white; cephalic and body setae moderate. Body length 3.5–4.50 mm. Head capsule subsquare (head length to mandibular base 1.0–1.10, maximum width 1.05–1.15 mm). Antennae 17-segmented, segment 3 shortest. Postclypeus inflated, setose, about half as long as wide. Pronotum saddle-shaped (length 0.40, width 0.63 mm), anterior margin weakly concave, posterior margin straight; meso- and metanotum as in the soldier. Minor worker: similar to the major worker but smaller, antennae 16–17-segmented; body length 3.0–3.60 mm, head length to mandibular base 0.70–0.80, maximum head width 0.78–0.90, pronotum length 0.30–0.40, width 0.50–0.60 mm.

sections.label: Alate
sections.text: Head capsule yellowish brown (recorded as dark brown by Holmgren and Holmgren 1917), antennae, labrum and postclypeus yellow-white (postclypeus tinged brown), pronotum yellowish brown with a paler T-shaped mark and shoulder spots, wings grey-brown, body yellowish brown. Cephalic and body setae dense. Body length (without wings) 11.6–12.3 mm. Head capsule subcircular, wider than long including compound eyes (head length to mandibular base 1.75–1.80, width including compound eyes 2.20–2.25 mm). Fontanelle small, at the centre of the head. Compound eyes subcircular (maximum diameter 0.60–0.63 mm), adjacent to the lower margin of the head. Ocelli broadly oval (long diameter 0.23–0.25, short diameter 0.20–0.23 mm), separated from the compound eye by less than their short diameter or slightly more than half their long diameter, and from the antenna by about their long diameter. Antennal segments 2 and 3 subequal, segment 3 subdivided, segment 4 shortest. Postclypeus strongly inflated, setose (length 0.5, width 1.0 mm). Pronotum subtrapezoidal (length 1.15–1.23, width 2.10–2.15 mm), anterior margin slightly upturned with a shallow median concavity, posterior margin straight, without a concavity.

sections.label: Other
sections.text: Roonwal and Bose (1961) described the subspecies O. b. guptai from specimens collected in Rajasthan, and Roonwal (1975) raised it to species rank. O. lokanandi, described by Chatterjee and Thakur (1967), was treated by Chhotani (1977) as a synonym of guptai. Thakur (1981) did not accept guptai and placed it in this species. After re-examining the various types, Chhotani maintained the earlier synonymy and considered this species to occur in peninsular India, whereas guptai occurs in the northern and north-eastern parts of the subcontinent (including Pakistan and Bangladesh).
